q: Purdue’s ultra-white paint reported in 2021 used a high concentration of which compound to scatter sunlight?
evidence: First-party report read: 2021 barium-sulfate formulation and varied particle sizes; avoids current record or availability claim.

q: Maryland researchers made nearly transparent panels by bleaching color-bearing structures and adding clear polymer to which normally opaque material?
evidence: Primary author-repository abstract and PDF read: modified lignin, chromophore removal, polymer infiltration, most lignin retained; thin wood panels.

q: The Nobel-winning experiments that isolated atom-thin graphene used which ordinary office supply to peel graphite apart?
evidence: Official prize scientific background read: tape peeling graphite 10–20 times, single-atom-thick carbon flakes.

q: What change in Bob Gore’s stretching experiments unexpectedly turned PTFE into the porous material behind early GORE-TEX fabrics?
evidence: Manufacturer historical account read: heated PTFE, sudden accelerating yank in October1969 produced microporous ePTFE; no universal statement for other polymers.

q: The material that became Silly Putty began as an unsuccessful attempt to replace what wartime-scarce substance?
evidence: Institutional materials entry read: silicone-based putty developed as failed natural-rubber substitute; uses date-neutral wording and avoids disputed sole-inventor credit.

q: What can a properly prepared Belousov–Zhabotinsky mixture do repeatedly after its ingredients have been combined?
evidence: University demonstration describes red–blue oscillations for hours and concentric patterns in a dish; no recipe supplied.

q: The transparent armor material ALON contains aluminum, yet belongs to which material class?
evidence: Manufacturer description read: ALON optical ceramic, transparent armor. Primary AlON research abstract also read; no unsupported performance numbers.

q: Pykrete, proposed for an extraordinary wartime aircraft carrier, strengthens ice by mixing it with what?
evidence: ACS experimental-history article read: original pykrete ice with wood pulp, proposed WWII carrier. Modern video tests other additives; question explicitly original material.

q: For a 2019 artwork, MIT’s ultrablack coating made which normally brilliant object look like a flat black void?
evidence: First-party report read: Redemption of Vanity, natural yellow diamond coated in CNT material. Date-scoped, no current-blackest claim.

q: A George Mason student prototype put out small flames using which surprising tool?
evidence: University research report read: student sound extinguisher, low-frequency bass worked rather than high frequency. Prototype scope; no household fire advice.

q: Duke’s 2014 pyramid-like cloak of perforated plastic was designed to hide an object from what?
evidence: First-party report read: plastic/air perforated stacked pyramid reroutes sound, flat-surface reflected wavefront; acoustic rather than visual invisibility.

q: A 2019 Sussex three-dimensional display drew luminous shapes in midair by rapidly moving what?
evidence: Primary abstract read: acoustically trapped particle, RGB illumination, rapid volume scanning. Tests moving image element, not duplicate food levitation mechanism.

q: In single-bubble sonoluminescence, what repeatedly drives a bubble to collapse and produce flashes of light?
evidence: Primary Nature abstract read: ultrasonically driven bubbles emit light on collapse; no fusion or unsupported temperature claim.

q: When sand forms intricate Chladni patterns on a vibrating plate, where does it collect?
evidence: Museum demonstration account read: sand displaced from moving areas accumulates at stationary nodes; no mystical sound-pattern claims.

q: In MIT’s 2014 visual-microphone demonstrations, recognizable speech was recovered by filming a small patch of which food package?
evidence: Authors’ research page read: speech recovered from192x192 20kHz video of small chip-bag patch. Other objects studied but not these three alternatives.

q: Alexander Graham Bell’s photophone transmitted speech without a connecting wire by varying what?
evidence: Primary Bell letter read: articulate speech produced by sunlight, selenium receiver variations of light as sounds, no conducting wire.

q: A 2019 research demonstration made certain voice-assistant microphones respond as if they heard speech, using which unexpected signal?
evidence: Authors’ page and primary paper abstract read: light-induced electrical audio response in tested MEMS microphones. Historic scope, no current-device claim or exploit procedure.

q: An optophone let a blind reader interpret ordinary printed letters by translating their shapes into what?
evidence: Original evaluation text read: six scanning spots across print, matching tones from black areas, reader deciphers shapes. Not speech synthesis or Braille.

q: A glassy polymer reported by Tokyo researchers in 2017 could repair a break at room temperature after what simple action?
evidence: Official Japanese research release read: polymer glass room-temperature pressure joining, special molecular structure, no heat melting. Avoid general claim for mineral glass.

q: UCLA researchers produced an X-ray image of a finger using what surprisingly ordinary object as the radiation source in a vacuum?
evidence: Primary abstract/editorial summary read: common tape peeled in vacuum generated nanosecondXrays and fingerimage; distinct from candy-visible-light triboluminescence, no instructions.

q: An Oregon State experiment on materials for electronics unexpectedly produced which useful artistic material in 2009?
evidence: First-party department history read: 2009 electronics research, bluecompound emerged after heating manganese-containing mixture. Avoid first-in200years claim.

q: Thomas Fogarty’s early balloon-catheter prototypes used an improvised balloon cut from what?
evidence: Inventor’s oral-history transcript read: baby finger of size5 glove, urethral catheter, fly-tying techniques. Historical description not medical instructions.

q: Willem Kolff’s early artificial-kidney work made ingenious use of which food-production material as a membrane?
evidence: Museum object history read: cellophane sausage casing and food tins, 1955–56 twin-coil example inapricottin. Avoid implying all prototypes samehousing.

q: Forensic laboratories can reveal latent fingerprints by exposing them to vapor from which familiar household product?
evidence: Official forensic manual chapter11 read: cyanoacrylate/superglue vapor forms clusters on latent residue; no operational instructions.

q: A car windshield can prevent many conventional photochromic eyeglasses from darkening strongly by blocking which part of sunlight?
evidence: Manufacturer technical explanation read: mostUV blocked windshield, conventionalphotochromic inadequate darkening; XTRActive responds visible too. No health or purchase recommendation.

q: An offer for an ivory substitute led John Wesley Hyatt toward an early plastic while he was trying to improve which objects?
evidence: Museum object account connects the ivory-replacement prize, Hyatt and celluloid billiard balls; does not claim he won the prize.

q: Which familiar kitchen smell can warn a film archivist that an old acetate film base is deteriorating?
evidence: Technical preservation document describes acetic-acid release, vinegar odor and acetate-film deterioration.

q: Which metal can slowly turn into a brittle gray powder through a cold-induced change in crystal structure, even without rusting?
evidence: Research introduction distinguishes white-to-gray tin transformation below about 13.2°C from corrosion; rate and initiation depend on conditions.

q: NASA warns that some tin-plated electronic parts can sprout what, potentially bridging contacts and causing a short circuit?
evidence: NASA guidance describes spontaneous conductive tin-whisker growth and short-circuit risk; not claiming only tin can form whiskers.

q: In a laboratory “chemical garden,” the branching structures that resemble underwater plants are actually what?
evidence: Primary paper introduction explicitly describes inorganic tubes, membrane formation, osmotic rupture and renewed tube growth.

q: In a 2001 self-healing polymer experiment, what hidden ingredient released repair liquid when an advancing crack broke it open?
evidence: Original abstract and figure description directly support microcapsule rupture, release and catalyst-triggered polymerization; no universal healing claim.

q: In a Caltech demonstration, a ball bearing bounced unusually well from a metal plate whose atoms lacked the usual orderly crystal pattern. What was the plate made of?
evidence: 1997 university article compares bearing rebounds from titanium and Liquidmetal; explains crystalline dislocations and energy loss.

q: A Los Alamos experiment cooled a specially doped glass fiber from room temperature to below freezing using what?
evidence: 1999 primary abstract reports glass-fiber cooling from 301 to 236 K in vacuum by anti-Stokes fluorescence; explanation limited to this special material.

q: What activates the small spikes in Harvard and MIT’s experimental kirigami shoe grips?
evidence: Institutional research summary and figure explain curvature-activated steel spikes; experimental footwear, not a retail claim.

q: Cambridge’s 2017 silk-inspired fibers were pulled from a gel that was overwhelmingly made of what?
evidence: University research report explicitly gives 98% water starting hydrogel and evaporation after drawing; avoids saying final dry fibers remain 98% water.

q: Harvard’s SLIPS coatings keep many liquids from sticking by holding what inside a porous solid surface?
evidence: Inventing institution describes porous micro/nanostructure infused with lubricating fluid; avoids marketing claims of universal repellency.

q: MIT’s 2023 cement-and-carbon-black research gave a building material which unexpected additional ability?
evidence: University report describes demonstrated supercapacitors and explicitly frames house foundations as a future application.

q: Cambridge researchers found that old cement paste could be recycled into new cement during which existing industrial process?
evidence: Developer’s process account explicitly explains electric-arc-furnace steel recycling, flux substitution and rapidly cooled slag; no zero-emissions claim.

q: McGill researchers made experimental glass slides much tougher by deliberately adding what?
evidence: University 2014 account describes patterned microcrack networks and optional polyurethane filling; no claim that random scratches strengthen glass.

q: A Bristol team’s 2012 experimental liquid soap could be pulled through another liquid by what?
evidence: First-party report describes magnetic iron-rich soap rising through an organic solvent in a test tube; cleanup uses remain proposed.

q: A University of Texas at Dallas team turned ordinary fishing line into artificial muscles chiefly by doing what to it?
evidence: Original 2014 abstract reports twist insertion, coiled polymer fibers, textile porosity and shutter demonstrations; heating supported by accompanying UT Dallas report.

q: A 2019 experimental cooling device chilled flowing water by changing what about solid fibers?
evidence: Original abstract describes twist-based cooling of flowing water and several fiber materials; does not imply all fibers cool with every twist direction.

q: A 2015 prototype motor used bacterial spores on plastic strips to harvest energy from which everyday process?
evidence: Funding institution describes evaporation-driven spore/polymer muscles, LEDs and miniature car; spores act through moisture response, not fuel digestion.

q: Northwestern researchers reported a graphene-based material in 2018 for coloring which everyday thing?
evidence: First-party account reports graphene oxide, wrapping hair, brown/black shades and wash tests; avoids unsupported safety/general commercial claims.

q: How did Northwestern’s half-millimeter robotic crab move in a 2022 demonstration?
evidence: Institutional report states scanned laser heating, shape-memory alloy and glass elastic return; no current smallest-record claim.

q: Writing made invisible by a FriXion pen’s heat-sensitive ink can often be brought back by what?
evidence: Manufacturer FAQ gives heat-triggered invisibility and color return below about −10°C; qualified can/often rather than guaranteed recovery.

q: In a 2023 materials demonstration, a tiny metal figure escaped a barred cage using which trick?
evidence: Original paper figure 1E and discussion show solid-liquid cage escape; does not suggest autonomous reassembly without external shaping.

q: In the Kaye effect, an incoming stream of shampoo can unexpectedly do what when it meets a pool of the liquid?
evidence: 2013 primary abstract identifies sideways/rebounding jet and directly observed lubricating air layer; no recipe or earlier disputed mechanism asserted.

q: When a suitable bead chain runs out of an elevated container, what surprising path can it take before falling to the floor?
evidence: Researcher’s institutional magazine account and photograph directly show arch above pot; avoids presenting one disputed force model as the whole explanation.

q: Cambridge research found that a kettle whistle at low flow could behave like which familiar sound-making object?
evidence: University account explicitly distinguishes low-flow Helmholtz resonance from higher-flow vortex mechanism; no all-kettle simplification.

q: A rattleback toy spun in its less-favored direction can wobble, stop and then do what without another push?
evidence: Institutional demo explicitly describes wrong-way rocking and reversal; no claim all designs reverse identically at all speeds.

q: What can a tippe top do after being spun rapidly on its rounded body?
evidence: University demonstration describes inversion and spinning on the stem, with energy transferred into raised center of mass.

q: Just before a spinning coin settles flat, what commonly happens to the pitch of its rapid rattling sound?
evidence: Paper’s directly observed phenomenon is rapidly increasing sound frequency before abrupt stop; avoids disputed claim air viscosity is the only dissipation mechanism.

q: Which physical process powers the repeated bobbing of a classic battery-free drinking-bird toy?
evidence: Demonstration explains humidity approaching saturation, head cooling ceasing and motion resuming after jar removal; toy needs no oxygen-burning motor.

q: In a 2024 experiment using ruby and two lasers, which apparently unlikely thing cast a visible shadow?
evidence: Publisher’s first-party research release specifies ruby, green and blue lasers, nonlinear absorption and shadow; not claiming beams cast shadows in ordinary empty air.

q: In a spectroscopy demonstration, a salt-containing flame can cast a dark shadow when illuminated by which light source?
evidence: University demo explicitly contrasts sodium-lamp shadow with no shadow under mercury lamp; absorption supported by University of Oregon matching demo.

q: Some home pregnancy-test strips use tiny particles of which precious metal as a visible label?
evidence: 2024 manufacturer submission pp5–8 describes colored lines and colloidal-gold-marked antibodies; statement scoped to some tests, no diagnostic advice.

q: In its 2005 research on Xerox DocuColor printers, EFF decoded identifying information hidden in what on printed pages?
evidence: Investigators’ guide explicitly documents yellow dot grids and decoded serial/date/time; does not universalize all printers or present current capability inventory.

q: What surrounded the flame in Humphry Davy’s miners’ safety lamp while still allowing light out?
evidence: Institution holding Davy’s lamp describes gauze enclosure and heat absorption; avoids absolute mine safety claim.

q: What chiefly drives the familiar rotation of a Crookes radiometer’s black-and-white vanes under a bright light?
evidence: Institutional demo explicitly distinguishes residual gas mechanism from photon momentum; wording avoids overprecise simplified edge-force explanation.

q: MIT researchers built reconfigurable miniature fluid-handling devices by cutting channels into which familiar objects?
evidence: First-party 2018 article describes actual micromilled commercial bricks and demonstrated module types; no assumed untreated-toy laboratory suitability.

q: Michelle Khine’s early low-cost microfluidics work used which craft product to shrink printed patterns into tiny molds?
evidence: 2007 university account describes CAD patterns printed on shrinking craft plastic, raised lines and PDMS molding.

q: Stanford’s Paperfuge adapted a string-powered whirligig toy to perform which laboratory job?
evidence: Inventing laboratory reports human-powered paper centrifuge and demonstrated plasma separation; no user procedure or medical recommendation.

q: A Tesla valve can resist liquid flow more strongly in one direction without using what conventional valve feature?
evidence: Primary paper describes asymmetric fixed geometry, direction-dependent fluid resistance and 1920 design; not an absolute one-way seal.

q: An industrial vortex tube can turn a single compressed-air supply into what pair of outputs without moving machinery inside it?
evidence: Manufacturer technical description directly states hot/cold streams from compressed air with no moving parts; no disputed detailed energy-separation theory used.

q: A Penn State prototype demonstrated at a Ben & Jerry’s shop kept ice cream cold using which unusual refrigeration tool?
evidence: University report states successful display-freezer demonstration and sound-driven compressed helium; not a claim that playing music freezes food.

q: What helps keep the magnetic top in a Levitron toy stable while it hovers above its base?
evidence: Institutional demo directly identifies spinning magnet levitated on another magnet and spin stabilization; permanent-magnet details corroborated by Saint Mary’s demo.

q: Researchers can make a short liquid-water bridge hang between two nearby beakers by applying what?
evidence: Primary abstract explicitly describes high voltage applied to pure water in nearby beakers and a spontaneously formed connection; no construction instructions.

q: Which extremely cold liquid can escape an open vessel by flowing as a thin film up the wall and over the rim?
evidence: Researcher’s Nobel lecture first page explicitly describes helium film climbing inner wall, passing rim and draining outer wall.

q: Which element remains liquid at ordinary pressure even when cooled extremely close to absolute zero?
evidence: Nobel lecture specifies solidification only with at least about25 atmospheres; distinct from film-flow question; avoids claiming absolute zero is experimentally attained.

q: In a vacuum-pump demonstration, water can first boil and then do what as the process continues?
evidence: University demonstration documents boiling followed by freezing; omits chemical apparatus and preparation instructions.

q: A miniature camera lens described by Philips researchers in 2004 changed focus by reshaping what?
evidence: Original paper abstract describes electrowetting of meniscus between immiscible liquids and demonstrated miniature camera module.

q: Even without a reflection of the sky, a long column of very pure water has a faint blue color chiefly because it absorbs which light more strongly?
evidence: Authors’ original experimental article reproduced in full: ultrapure/distilled water spectra and red-end absorption; no claim every lake’s color has only one cause.

q: A material nicknamed “dry water” can flow like a powder even though each grain contains what?
evidence: First-person account by Liverpool researcher describes liquid droplets, hydrophobic silica coating and powder behavior; no gas-storage fact repeated from methane hydrate.

q: When the top of a freely hanging, settled Slinky is released, what does its bottom end initially do?
evidence: Researcher’s primary mathematical account models the bottom remaining stationary until compression arrives; almost qualification allows real-spring deviations.

q: An early home experiment behind Pyrex cookware involved baking a sponge cake in the cut-off bottom of what?
evidence: Museum history describes Jesse Littleton bringing home sawn-off Nonex battery-jar bottoms and Bessie baking a sponge cake in one.

q: The chemist behind Super Glue encountered its stubbornly sticky ingredients while investigating plastics for what wartime equipment?
evidence: Hall of Fame biography states Coover tested cyanoacrylates during World War II as clear plastic for precision gunsights.

q: Before WD-40 became a household spray, an early customer used it to protect the outer skin of what?
evidence: Company history identifies Convair and the Atlas missile outer skin as the first commercial application.

q: What does the 40 in WD-40 commemorate?
evidence: Company history explicitly identifies the fortieth attempt to perfect a water-displacement formula.

q: Before nylon became famous for stockings, which everyday product used its bristles commercially?
evidence: Museum record and donor account identify nylon toothbrush bristles as the first commercial nylon product; conflicting catalog dates are deliberately omitted.

q: According to Edwin Land’s account, what request from his young daughter helped spark his work on instant photography?
evidence: Institute biography recounts Land’s daughter asking why she could not see the picture immediately; no disputed year is asserted.

q: Which kitchen staple did Cornell engineers put inside prototype robot fingers to make them curl when heated?
evidence: University report describes three-finger silicone grippers containing heated kernels, expansion-driven curling, and the generally one-use limitation. This tests robotic use, not the published steam-in-popcorn fact.

q: What kind of ink helped inspire László Bíró to develop his practical ballpoint pen?
evidence: Hall of Fame account connects his journalism, quick-drying newspaper ink, and the problem of using thick ink in a fountain pen.

q: Harry Brearley’s work toward rust-resistant steel began with efforts to improve which item, rather than kitchen cutlery?
evidence: Archival research describes the 1912 rifle-barrel erosion investigation and subsequent chromium-steel development; sole-inventor and disputed discovery-date claims are avoided.

q: An accidental spill during research on aircraft fuel-line rubber helped inspire Scotchgard. What had the stubborn mixture landed on?
evidence: Smithsonian describes the rubber-mixture spill on shoes and resistance to washing. A 3M history differs on the wearer and year, so neither detail is used.

q: The ribbed shape that inspired Coca-Cola’s contour bottle came from the fruit of which plant?
evidence: Company history describes Root Glass researchers finding the ribbed cocoa fruit illustration. Its imprecise term cocoa bean is rendered botanically as fruit rather than copied.

q: Earl Tupper modeled the seal on his plastic food containers after the lid of what?
evidence: Museum object description explicitly says Tupper modeled the lid after a paint-can lid.

q: Alfred Nobel made nitroglycerin easier to handle by combining it with which absorbent material in early dynamite?
evidence: Nobel Foundation account names kieselguhr, or diatomaceous earth, as the absorbent. No recipe, quantities, or handling instructions are included.

q: A North Carolina State armor experiment pulverized an incoming armor-piercing bullet using a composite that incorporated which unusually airy material?
evidence: University report describes composite armor using metal foam and an armor-piercing projectile shattered in a documented test; no claim that foam alone was the entire armor.

q: Litracon concrete can show the shadow of someone standing behind it. What carries light through the solid-looking blocks?
evidence: Materials-library description identifies carefully arranged optical fibers running through Litracon blocks.

q: Matter of Trust turns donated salon hair clippings into felted mats designed to clean up what?
evidence: Manufacturer/nonprofit technical flyer documents felted hair products for oil spills and surface adsorption; no comparative efficiency claim.

q: A 2021 materials study demonstrated a knife that could cut steak despite being made mainly from what?
evidence: Primary study reports a hardened-wood table knife; publisher release documents steak-cutting demonstration. Avoids overstating the comparison as sharper than all steel knives.

q: In experiments inspired by spider silk junctions, ordinary adhesive-tape joints could become much harder to peel apart by changing what?
evidence: Primary paper abstract identifies intersection angle as controlling weak versus self-strengthening tape-junction behavior.

q: Cornell researchers built soft robotic fingers that dealt with excess heat using which surprisingly lifelike trick?
evidence: University account describes temperature-dependent pores, hydrogel water release, and evaporative cooling in a 2020 soft-robot prototype.

q: Harvard’s 2016 octobot moved its soft arms without batteries or rigid motors. What powered their movement?
evidence: First-party report explicitly identifies reaction-generated pressurized gas and microfluidic controls in the untethered proof-of-concept robot.

q: MIT’s 2016 experimental origami robot was designed to unfold in a stomach. What material formed its outer structural layers?
evidence: University report describes dried pig intestine outer layers and a Biolefin inner layer; demonstrations used a simulated stomach.

q: A Stanford soft robot demonstrated in 2017 could advance through clutter while much of its body stayed still. How did its front move forward?
evidence: University account describes pressurized thin plastic folded inside itself, eversion at the tip, and a stationary body.

q: In a 2019 storage experiment, Microsoft and Warner Bros. recovered the entire 1978 Superman film from a coaster-sized slab of what?
evidence: First-party account identifies 75-by-75-by-2-millimeter quartz glass, complete film storage/retrieval, and laser-written internal structures in a proof of concept.

q: Rice University’s 2005 single-molecule nanocar had four wheels made from what?
evidence: University report identifies four C60 wheels and scanning-tunneling-microscope tests of rolling on gold.

q: A strong magnet falls surprisingly slowly through a copper tube even though copper does not stick to a fridge magnet. What causes the braking?
evidence: University demonstration explains the slow fall through copper as eddy-current magnetic braking; contrast with a nonconducting tube.

q: In experiments with an oil droplet bouncing on a vibrating oil bath, what can steer the droplet as it appears to walk across the surface?
evidence: MIT experiment describes bouncing oil droplets propelled and guided by their self-generated waves. This is a classical analogue, not proof of a quantum interpretation.

q: NC State researchers made experimental wires that could reconnect after being cut and pressed together. What unusual material carried electricity inside them?
evidence: First-party report identifies liquid gallium–indium channels inside self-healing polymer and reconnection after severed ends are reunited.

q: In a 2020 fluid-physics experiment, small model boats floated upside down beneath a suspended liquid layer. What kept this strange arrangement stable?
evidence: Primary experiment reports inverted buoyancy under vertical shaking. Its linked correction changes a reference-author surname only, not the result.

q: Rice researchers showed that used coffee grounds and other carbon-rich waste could be transformed by brief intense electrical heating into what valuable material?
evidence: University report explicitly describes flash Joule heating of carbon sources and coffee grounds yielding graphene; speculative cost and environmental claims omitted.

q: MIT Lincoln Laboratory demonstrated a laser system that delivered sound near a listener’s ear without headphones. Which substance in the air absorbed the light to create sound?
evidence: Laboratory technology description identifies ambient water vapor as the absorber and photoacoustic conversion as the mechanism.

q: Some carbon-nanotube loudspeakers produce sound without a vibrating speaker cone. What directly disturbs the surrounding air?
evidence: Primary paper explains nanotube thermoacoustics and reports no sheet mechanical vibration detected by a laser vibrometer.

q: An MIT camera system reconstructed objects hidden around a corner by treating what ordinary surface as an indirect reflector?
evidence: University account describes reconstruction using diffusely reflecting ordinary walls rather than mirror-like surfaces.

q: A Stanford computer prototype reported in 2015 represented and manipulated bits using what moving objects?
evidence: First-party report describes synchronous droplet logic, nanoparticle-loaded water droplets, and a rotating magnetic clock.

q: In a 2019 Boston University experiment, what shape of acoustic device quieted a tone while leaving an open air passage?
evidence: First-party annual-report project describes an open acoustic metamaterial cutting a tone while preserving air passage; no unsupported broadband claim.

q: Empa’s disposable paper-battery prototype could be switched on by adding what?
evidence: Institutional 2022 report describes water activation, salt dissolution, printed electrodes, and the alarm-clock proof of concept.

q: MIT’s PhotoChromeleon experiment could replace a colorful pattern on a coated shoe or phone case without repainting it. What reprogrammed the coating?
evidence: University report describes cyan, magenta, and yellow photochromic dyes controlled by UV light and projected visible light.

q: When an auxetic material is stretched lengthwise, how can its overall width respond in contrast to an ordinary rubber band?
evidence: Institutional research explanation states longitudinal stretching causes lateral expansion; ordinary elastics narrow. No medical-use claim is tested.

q: JILA researchers measured a gravitational difference in ticking rates within a single cloud of atoms in 2022. Roughly how far apart vertically were its top and bottom?
evidence: NIST reports gravitational frequency differences across roughly one millimeter within a single strontium cloud. The tested fact is experimental resolution, not the general time-dilation principle already in earth003.

q: Albert Einstein and Leo Szilard worked on a safer version of which household appliance after concerns about lethal gas leaks?
evidence: Smithsonian account documents their refrigeration project, toxic refrigerant leaks, hermetically sealed pump, and commercialization difficulties.

q: In a disappearing-glass demonstration, a clear rod becomes almost invisible when immersed in a particular liquid. Which property must the rod and liquid closely match?
evidence: Museum exhibit explanation attributes disappearance to matching refractive indices; a rod of different glass remains visible.

q: Rice’s 2022 necrobotics experiment turned which deceased creatures into miniature mechanical grippers?
evidence: University account describes deceased wolf spiders used as pressure-actuated grippers; this tests an engineering application rather than general spider anatomy.

q: Cornell’s microscopic nanoguitar demonstrated in 2003 was played using what instead of a musician’s fingers?
evidence: University article title explicitly states laser-played; body identifies silicon-bar strings and vibrations 17 octaves above ordinary guitar frequencies.

q: Swedish researchers demonstrated a working transistor in 2023 using which unexpected structural material infused with a conducting polymer?
evidence: First-party university account specifies delignified balsa filled with PEDOT:PSS and a working current-regulating transistor; no first-ever or commercial-replacement claim.

q: Canada’s NRC used a special impact simulator to fire which unusual projectiles at aircraft components?
evidence: Contemporary government report page61 explicitly describes pre-killed birds fired to duplicate in-flight collisions; no frozen-chicken urban legend.

q: A robotic gripper reported by Cornell and collaborators in 2010 used a party balloon filled with which lightweight material?
evidence: University account documents selected coffee-filled latex balloon and vacuum-triggered granular jamming. Rice and couscous were also tested, so neither is a distractor.

q: Lancaster physicists found that structures made from which familiar toy could act as unusually effective thermal insulators at very low temperatures?
evidence: Primary paper measures LEGO ABS/void structures from70mK to1.8K and reports strong thermal isolation with mechanical support; no room-temperature extrapolation.

q: For a 2012 airplane wireless-signal test, Boeing filled passenger seats with sacks of what as stand-ins for people?
evidence: Manufacturer’s dated release documents potato sacks in a grounded decommissioned aircraft and subsequent human validation.

q: A physics team studied how nonspherical objects pack together by filling containers with which familiar sweets?
evidence: Primary paper describes regular and mini M&M experiments and higher random packing fractions than ball bearings; comparison does not claim superiority to optimally ordered spheres.

q: Cambridge researchers demonstrated a way to make toner-printed office paper reusable without turning it back into pulp. What removed the print?
evidence: Institutional study account documents tests of laser toner removal on standard copy paper, analysis of damage, and the reuse concept.

q: A 2022 MIT and Rhode Island School of Design project made a washable shirt fabric function as what?
evidence: First-party study report describes piezoelectric fiber, machine-washable cloth, acoustic detection, and clap-direction demonstration. No clinical performance claim.

q: Which liquid helped a laboratory bubble survive for more than a year by compensating for water lost to evaporation?
evidence: Institutional report describes a 465-day particle-armored bubble; glycerol absorbs atmospheric water and counters evaporation.

q: Rochester researchers made water climb a metal surface without a pump in 2009. What modification helped it happen?
evidence: First-party report describes femtosecond-laser surface structures, guided flow, and upward wicking without a pump.

q: A 2022 University of Maryland battery used a gel derived from which discarded seafood material?
evidence: First-party report identifies crab-shell chitosan as the basis of a biodegradable zinc-battery electrolyte.

q: Stanford’s experimental cooling cloth was opaque to visible light but allowed which kind of radiation from the body to escape?
evidence: First-party 2016 report distinguishes visible opacity and infrared transmission and describes a skin-temperature device test.

q: In a 2022 SLAC experiment, an intense laser shock helped turn which familiar packaging material into nanodiamonds?
evidence: First-party experiment report identifies PET plastic and X-ray evidence of nanodiamond formation under laser-driven shock compression.

q: Viewed between polarizing filters, a loaded clear plastic model can reveal otherwise invisible patterns of what?
evidence: Museum exhibit describes a clear plastic femur whose stress becomes visible between polarizing sheets when force is applied.

q: If half of a conventional holographic plate is covered, what can the uncovered portion still show?
evidence: Museum explanation states that hiding half a hologram still leaves the whole object visible. No claim of unchanged viewing range or quality.

q: The protective material D3O stays flexible during ordinary movement but resists deformation much more during what?
evidence: Manufacturer technical article describes rate-sensitive response, energy absorption during impact, and return to flexibility. Avoids literal molecular-locking metaphor.

q: The 2014 Rochester optical cloak hid objects over a limited viewing range using four ordinary examples of what?
evidence: First-party report identifies four standard lenses and continuous but limited viewing angles.

q: A 2021 experiment briefly gave a thin layer of which familiar liquid a metallic, golden appearance by supplying it with electrons?
evidence: Institutional study report describes an electron-rich aqueous layer on sodium-potassium alloy, golden color, and spectroscopic evidence of metallic behavior.

q: What was unusual about Berkeley Lab’s magnetic liquid droplets after the external magnetizing field was removed in 2019?
evidence: First-party report distinguishes permanently magnetic droplets from ordinary ferrofluids and explains the role of jammed iron-oxide nanoparticles.

q: A bar of tin can make a crackling “cry” when bent. What produces the sound?
evidence: University element demonstration explicitly attributes tin cry to deformation twinning.

q: Zirconium tungstate is unusual because, over a substantial temperature range, heating can make it do what?
evidence: Institutional research report describes zirconium tungstate as a prototype isotropic negative-thermal-expansion material across a broad temperature range.

q: An MIT microscopy technique made fine structures easier to see by doing what to the prepared tissue itself?
evidence: Research image explanation describes tissue embedded in hydrogel, physical magnification in all directions, and improved optical resolution.

q: Why can molten sulfur become dramatically thicker over part of its heating range instead of simply getting runnier?
evidence: Research thesis describes the viscosity rise near the sulfur polymerization transition and formation of long chains; no claim of thickening at every temperature.

q: The discovery of liquid crystals began with a puzzling cloudy phase in compounds derived from which substance?
evidence: Institute history identifies cholesterol acetate and benzoate, cloudy intermediate liquid, and a second transition to clear liquid.

q: A 2014 chemistry study repurposed which packing material as an array of little containers for laboratory tests?
evidence: Primary study abstract describes bubble-wrap compartments for liquid storage and analytical assays, including glucose and hemoglobin.

q: Which natural material helped Tufts researchers preserve heat-sensitive vaccines in dry experimental films in a 2012 study?
evidence: First-party study report describes silk-fibroin films preserving vaccine potency during elevated-temperature storage experiments.

q: The DuoSkin research project turned decorative temporary tattoos into touch controls using which conductive craft material?
evidence: Primary 2016 paper identifies gold leaf, tattoo paper, touch sensors, and near-field communication demonstrations.

q: Ray McIntire’s work toward what wartime substitute unexpectedly led to the foam sold as STYROFOAM?
evidence: Inventor profile identifies wartime rubber shortage, flexible-insulator goal, styrene/isobutylene experiment, and foam formation.

q: A diamond battery announced by UK researchers in 2024 draws energy from what process?
evidence: UKAEA first-party announcement identifies a carbon-14 diamond battery and energy from radioactive decay; applications remain prospective.

q: In a UT Dallas demonstration, specially made yarn sewn into a shirt generated electricity from which ordinary action?
evidence: First-party 2017 report explicitly describes shirt-sewn twistron yarn stretched by normal breathing and generating an electrical signal.

q: A small MIT airplane flew indoors in 2018 without propellers or turbines. What supplied its thrust?
evidence: First-party report and linked primary paper describe electroaerodynamic thrust, onboard power, and sustained indoor flight without moving propulsion parts.

q: MIT researchers made bacteria retain records of chemical exposure in 2014 by writing changes into what?
evidence: First-party report describes engineered E. coli genomic memory, recorded chemical exposure, and inheritance of the record across generations.

q: In MIT’s experimental all-liquid battery, what keeps the molten metal and salt components arranged in separate layers?
evidence: First-party 2014 report explicitly attributes three self-separated liquid layers to different densities.

q: UMass Amherst’s 2020 Air-gen device generated electricity from which normally overlooked feature of the surrounding air?
evidence: First-party report and primary PMID 32066937 identify atmospheric water vapor and a self-maintained moisture gradient in protein-nanowire films.

q: What controlled the movements of CUHK’s experimental “slimebot,” which could squeeze through gaps and wrap around objects?
evidence: First-party 2022 report describes externally magnetically controlled slime, gap navigation, and battery-encircling demonstration in a stomach model.

q: MIT’s see-through solar-cell research aimed to harvest which parts of sunlight while letting most visible light pass?
evidence: Institutional research explanation explicitly describes ultraviolet and near-infrared absorption with low visible absorption.

q: What supplied the force that moved the fingers of MIT’s transparent hydrogel fish-gripper in 2017?
evidence: First-party report identifies mostly-water hydrogel, water-pumped actuation, underwater camouflage, and fish-gripping demonstration.

q: Early HASEL artificial muscles at CU Boulder contained which supermarket liquid inside their flexible pouches?
evidence: Institutional report explicitly identifies supermarket canola oil, electrostatic displacement, and recovery from dielectric breakdown.

q: A Harvard–MIT robot began as a flat sheet, folded itself, then walked away in 2014. What triggered its folds?
evidence: First-party report distinguishes electrical leads heating joints from earlier oven-heated prototypes and describes autonomous folding followed by walking.

q: In a famous 1999 experiment, which kind of pulse was slowed to roughly 38 miles per hour inside an ultracold gas?
evidence: Primary paper reports optical pulse propagation at 17 metres per second through an ultracold sodium gas; 38 mph is a rounded conversion.

q: Yale’s 2011 device could make suitably matched incoming laser beams almost entirely disappear into an absorber. What was its popular nickname?
evidence: First-party report identifies the anti-laser nickname, coherent perfect absorber, silicon wafer, matched incoming beams, and heat generation.

q: University of Chicago physicists used shaped underwater wings in 2013 to tie knots in what?
evidence: First-party report describes 3-D-printed hydrofoils making water vortex knots and their reconnection dynamics.

q: In 2011, researchers used a single living cell containing fluorescent protein as the light-amplifying part of what device?
evidence: Primary paper reports GFP-expressing live cells in an optical cavity, externally pumped laser emission, and survival after prolonged lasing.

q: A study of the Alhambra traced unexpected purple patches in its gilded decoration to tiny particles of which metal?
evidence: Primary 2022 conservation study identifies gold nanoparticles as the cause of purple discoloration in gilded Alhambra decoration.

q: Some heated crystals suddenly leap off a hotplate. What supplies the mechanical kick in the thermosalient effect?
evidence: Institutional study explanation attributes jumping to rapid release of mechanical tension during a structural phase change.

q: The “metallic” smell left on your hand after touching iron largely comes from reactions involving what?
evidence: First-party report identifies metal-induced oxidation of skin lipids and odor-producing aldehydes and ketones.

q: Harvard’s 2013 soft jumping robot got its sudden upward kick from what?
evidence: First-party report describes combustion-driven pressure inside silicone channels producing repeated jumps; no construction instructions included.

q: In MIT’s “fluid trampoline” experiment, a water droplet bounced repeatedly on what thin vibrating surface?
evidence: First-party report describes water drops bouncing on a vertically vibrating soap film; primary follow-up paper details the fluid system.

q: For IBM’s 2013 stop-motion film, the animators physically repositioned which microscopic objects between frames?
evidence: Film director’s first-party project description identifies carbon monoxide molecules, scanning tunneling microscopy, and frame-by-frame repositioning.

q: Caltech researchers made nanoscale smiley faces by folding long strands of what material with shorter molecular “staples”?
evidence: Researcher’s own description specifies a long DNA strand, short folding strands, and nanoscale smiley-face structures.

q: A special drill based on a rounded triangular shape can cut a hole that is approximately what shape?
evidence: Primary fabrication paper reports Reuleaux-triangle geometry, constrained moving center, and removal of 98.7 percent of the desired square area.

q: How many stable resting positions does an ideal uniform-density Gömböc have on a level surface?
evidence: Museum object description identifies homogeneous material, exactly one stable and one unstable equilibrium, and shape-based self-righting.

q: Davy and Faraday’s experiment in Florence showed that which precious stone could keep burning in pure oxygen once ignited?
evidence: Primary Faraday text recounts Davy’s Florence experiment and continued combustion of diamond in oxygen after removal of the original heat source.

q: What hidden component lets a heated Rijke tube keep roaring briefly after the flame is removed?
evidence: University demonstration description identifies internal wire gauze and sustained roaring from retained heat after removal from a flame.

q: A 2021 study made flexible microfibers from which normally brittle material, allowing them to bend and spring back while very cold?
evidence: Primary paper reports reversible bending of single-crystal ice microfibers under cryogenic conditions, approaching the theoretical elastic limit.

q: Washington State researchers made experimental memory components in 2022 using a solidified layer of which sweet substance?
evidence: First-party report identifies solidified honey between electrodes and measured memristor switching and synapse-like responses, not a complete artificial brain.

q: Form Energy’s iron-air battery takes advantage of a reversible version of which familiar process?
evidence: Manufacturer’s technical description explicitly identifies reversible rusting and the charge/discharge transformations; no price or performance forecast used.

q: In the MycelioTronics study, researchers grew a biodegradable support for electronic circuits from what?
evidence: Primary 2022 paper reports fungal mycelium skins as substrates, deposited conducting traces, flexible circuits, and autonomous sensing demonstrations.

q: NASA’s early ferrofluid research tried to use magnets to guide which troublesome liquid inside a spacecraft?
evidence: NASA history describes Papell’s magnetic propellant concept, pump-intake guidance in low gravity, and eventual choice of simpler methods.

q: A 2018 MIT fog collector pulled tiny airborne water droplets toward its collecting mesh by giving them what?
evidence: Primary study abstract describes space-charge injection, net droplet charge, and electric-field-guided collection.

q: What physical effect makes magnetostriction a source of hum in an electrical transformer?
evidence: Engineering documentation explicitly describes magnetization-induced dimensional changes and the resulting transformer hum; replacement avoids original university host’s certificate error.

q: Some originally clear antique glass develops a purple tint after long exposure to what?
evidence: Museum glass-science explanation identifies sunlight/UV-induced purple coloration in glass decolorized with manganese compounds.

q: On a conventional safety-match box, which part contains the red phosphorus needed for striking?
evidence: Museum specimen materials identify potassium chlorate in heads and red phosphorus in the striking medium; no mixture amounts or making instructions used.

q: Some supermarket barcode-scanner windows are protected by a scratch-resistant layer of which synthetic gemstone material?
evidence: Primary patent describes commercial sapphire/glass scanning windows and explicitly identifies scratch resistance as their purpose.

q: A miniature caterpillar-like robot made from liquid-crystal elastomer could inch along under which external energy source?
evidence: Primary paper describes a monolithic liquid-crystal-elastomer film, visible-light excitation, and inching on paper and a blazed grating.

q: In classic black-and-white E Ink displays, the page image is made by moving what toward the viewing surface?
evidence: Manufacturer describes microcapsules, black and white charged pigments, clear fluid, and electric-field-driven particle movement.

q: Percy Shaw’s self-cleaning Cat’s Eye road studs used passing tires to help wash the reflectors with what?
evidence: Museum educational account describes a rainwater-collecting base and tire pressure depressing the block to clean its reflectors.

q: James Dewar developed his 1892 vacuum flask mainly to preserve which kind of laboratory material?
evidence: Institution holding the flask explains its development for cryogenic research and slowing evaporation of liquefied gases.

q: What provides the ignition heat in a fire piston, without a flame or spark?
evidence: University demonstration explains increased gas temperature under rapid compression and explicitly connects the effect to diesel ignition.

q: Stanford researchers built a pocket microscope around a surprisingly simple structural material. What formed the Foldscope’s main body?
evidence: Primary 2014 paper describes folded-paper structural loops, passive optical alignment, flexure mechanisms, and portable microscopy.

q: The hand-cranked chain saw called Heine’s osteotome was designed for work on what?
evidence: Custodian museum identifies a surgical chainsaw and cites its purpose as joint-surface resection through relatively small incisions. Does not repeat unsupported childbirth origin.

q: An ordinary flat mirror is often said to swap left and right. Which direction does its geometry actually reverse?
evidence: Museum’s Going Further section explicitly explains flat-mirror reversal as in/out, with the apparent right/left relation depending on orientation.

q: The cushioning material now called memory foam grew out of NASA work to improve what?
evidence: NASA first-party history explicitly identifies commercial airplane passenger-seat safety as the origin, distinguishing it from later spacecraft uses.

q: Some self-lit EXIT signs glow without wires or batteries because they contain which radioactive gas?
evidence: EPA explanation identifies tritium beta decay, phosphor light emission, and operation without conventional electrical power.

q: Walter Jaeger’s early device unexpectedly responded to cigarette smoke while he was trying to detect what?
evidence: Regulator’s historical account describes a late-1930s poison-gas sensor responding when Jaeger lit a cigarette.

q: To study how atoms rearrange when a metal surface is dented, an MIT team built a much larger model out of what?
evidence: MIT institutional report describes a one-layer bubble raft modeling nanoindentation and surface defects; its measured behavior matched metal experiments.

q: A 2011 experimental 3-D printer tested in the desert fused sand into glass objects using which heat source?
evidence: Custodian museum and designer’s project page describe sunlight and sand, desert testing, layered 3-D printing, and the resulting bowl.

q: Cloudflare has used footage of which decorative objects as an extra source of randomness for internet security?
evidence: Company’s technical explanation explicitly describes lava-lamp camera footage and mixing its data with other entropy sources.

q: The Cray-2 supercomputer kept its densely packed electronics cool by placing them directly in what?
evidence: Original manufacturer brochure describes direct liquid immersion in an insulating fluorocarbon coolant, including integrated circuits and power supplies.

q: A 2015 experimental heat engine generated rotation and electrical power using levitating blocks of what?
evidence: University authors explain demonstrated dry-ice rotors hovering on their vapor above heated surfaces; vapor drives rotation converted into power. Tested fact is the solid working material.

q: A laser beam can follow a curving stream of water from a bottle because of what optical effect?
evidence: University demonstration explicitly describes laser light trapped in a water stream by total internal reflection.

q: A NIST schlieren photograph of an ordinary warm hand made what normally invisible feature visible?
evidence: NIST research image caption describes its own schlieren optical system revealing refractive-index gradients and heat-driven airflow from a human hand.

q: In traditional vat dyeing with indigo, what makes the dye regain its blue color after the cloth leaves the bath?
evidence: University chemistry explanation identifies soluble leucoindigo and atmospheric reoxidation restoring the insoluble blue dye. No claim about indigo word origin used.

q: Australian researchers made inexpensive microscope lenses by hanging droplets and baking them. What were the droplets made from?
evidence: Publisher’s 2014 research release describes transparent PDMS silicone droplets shaped by hanging and cured in an oven; phone attachments were demonstrated.

q: One Deciwatt lamp can run without batteries or sunshine after a user lifts a weighted bag. What powers it afterward?
evidence: First-person product-development account explains lifting the bag, slow descent, gear train, and generator; power is stored human work, not free energy.

q: A key strengthening step for Gorilla Glass involves giving it a hot bath in what?
evidence: Manufacturer describes molten-salt ion exchange: larger potassium ions replace sodium ions and create surface compression.

q: Compared with an identical glow stick at room temperature, what usually happens when an activated glow stick is warmed?
evidence: ACS comparison explains temperature-dependent reaction rates, stronger brightness when warm, and shorter duration.

q: A NIST-led team studied an alloy in 2009 that could be cooled by removing what, after first allowing it to shed heat?
evidence: NIST describes magnetocaloric heating in a magnetic field, heat rejection, and cooling when that field is removed.

q: In a 2016 MIT experiment, which grocery-store plant became part of a system that detected explosive-related chemicals and sent email alerts?
evidence: Institutional report directly identifies spinach, embedded nanotube nitroaromatic sensors, groundwater uptake, infrared camera, and computer-generated email. This is engineering, not natural plant email.

q: In NYU’s low-friction tests, a submerged sprinkler sucked water inward instead of spraying it out. How did its rotation compare with an ordinary sprinkler?
evidence: Courant’s research report explicitly states opposite rotation at much slower speed in submerged suction experiments; date not tested because institutional page metadata is inconsistent with earlier reporting.

q: The “flint” in a typical disposable cigarette lighter is usually made from what?
evidence: RSC chemist explains that lighter flints are ferrocerium alloy, not silicon-dioxide stone, and scraped particles ignite.

q: Which building material can be supplied inside a flexible fabric roll, then hardened into a durable lining by adding water?
evidence: Manufacturer’s technical manager describes flexible concrete-filled fabric that hardens on hydration and is used for canal and ditch linings.

q: ETH Zurich researchers describe a friction-welding method for joining pieces of which familiar construction material?
evidence: ETH research description states that linear friction heats timber interfaces, leading to melting and fusion across a stable bondline.

q: A stretched rubber band supporting a small weight is gently warmed in a physics demonstration. What unexpected movement can occur?
evidence: University demonstration explicitly warms a weighted stretched band and measures its contraction; material explanation also supported by University of Washington MatEd module.

q: At Coperni’s 2022 runway show, Fabrican created Bella Hadid’s white dress directly on her body using what?
evidence: Technology developer’s account identifies its team spraying the dress onto the model, followed by cutting the straps and slit.

q: A specially manufactured form of which material can float above an arrangement of permanent magnets at room temperature?
evidence: University demonstration uses thin pyrolytic graphite over nine neodymium cube magnets and explicitly attributes levitation to diamagnetism.

q: On Pilkington Activ self-cleaning glass, how is rain encouraged to behave so it can carry dirt away?
evidence: Manufacturer explains hydrophilic sheeting and UV-driven photocatalytic breakdown of organic deposits; water-repellent beading is a different surface strategy.

q: In a 2026 study of squeaks, researchers played the Star Wars theme by sliding specially shaped pieces of what along glass?
evidence: Institutional report states differently sized rubber blocks were designed to play the Star Wars theme by hand; block height controls frequency.

q: In 2019 experiments, crystals of neopentylglycol showed large thermal changes that suggested a solid refrigerant. What triggered those changes?
evidence: Primary abstract and introduction identify large pressure-driven thermal changes near room temperature due to molecular reconfiguration.

q: MIT’s 2022 paper-thin loudspeaker could still work when attached to a rigid wall. What moved to make its sound?
evidence: Institutional report explains individually vibrating piezoelectric domes and protective spacer layers; distinguishes this design from whole-film vibration.

q: How did NC State’s twisted, pasta-shaped soft robots get around obstacles in maze experiments without a computer directing them?
evidence: Primary institutional report describes thermal rolling, physical rotation or snapping on contact, and maze navigation without software or human control.

q: One design for airliner passenger oxygen masks makes oxygen on demand. What produces it?
evidence: Official investigation section1.6.5.5 describes modular passenger oxygen produced by sodium-chlorate decomposition with heat; question explicitly limited to chemical-generator aircraft.

q: Why did metrologists polish almost perfectly round spheres of exceptionally pure silicon?
evidence: National metrology institute describes calculating silicon atom counts from sphere volume and crystal unit-cell volume, then relating that count to mass.

q: High-speed imaging in Harvard’s 2026 squeaky-rubber study sometimes caught what surprising event at the sliding contact?
evidence: Same institutional report explicitly records triboelectric discharges sometimes triggering opening slip pulses. Distinct from the musical-block demonstration.

q: UCL’s 2024 “nanopasta” research pulled flour-based threads through a needle using what?
evidence: Institutional report identifies electrospinning, electric charge pulling flour/formic-acid mixture through needle, and nonculinary nanofiber research.

q: In Rice’s 2016 “Teslaphoresis” demonstration, what assembled itself into wires that connected and powered two LEDs?
evidence: Research team’s institutional report explicitly describes nanotube wires self-assembling into a two-LED circuit and harvesting power from the Tesla-coil field.

q: Some experimental self-healing asphalt contains which kitchen-scrubber material so an electromagnetic field can heat it and close small cracks?
evidence: Authors’ research review explains steel-wool fibers, induction currents, and capillary flow/diffusion of heated bitumen closing microcracks; not bacterial concrete or capsule repair.

q: Where did NIST collect the material used in its carefully measured household-dust reference sample?
evidence: NIST states the house dust was collected from vacuum cleaner bags across six US states; source also explains contaminant analysis. Question tests sample origin, not orbital transport.
